chapters.title: Chapter 16 · Amy and the Limes
chapters.artPrompt: a small girl in a neat school dress standing mortified on a platform in front of a classroom of smirking pupils while a stern teacher holds up a basket of green limes, rows of wooden desks and tall windows, cold morning light, gentle storybook illustration

blocks.text: At Amy’s school, pickled limes were more precious than gold. The girls traded them, lent them at interest, and gossiped over them like little merchants. Amy had none, and was poor in lime, which she felt as deeply as any beggar. Then a kind friend gave her a whole basket. For one shining day Amy shared her riches grandly. She was queen of the school, and the world smelled of sharp green sweetness. The limes came in little paper twists, and were worth whole libraries of friendship.
Mr. Davis holds the forbidden basket high while the whole school looks on.

But the master, Mr. Davis, hated limes and all their works. He seized Amy’s basket in front of everyone. He rapped her knuckles and made her stand on the platform with it, like a little prisoner. Amy’s cheeks burned, her heart broke, and she came home in tears to tell the whole tale. Mother listened quietly. Her face grew grave as she heard. A school that shames a child over limes teaches her something worse than sums. The whole school had laughed, and the laugh cut deeper than the rapped knuckles.
Talk together: one small fruit made Amy queen for a day and prisoner the next. What silly things rule classrooms today?

Mother decided that this was not the school for Amy. “You shall rest at home awhile,” she said, “and study with Aunt March.” Amy received this sentence with great tragedy, for Aunt March was stern and her house was stiff. But there was no help for it. She dried her eyes, packed her little trunk, and went, like a brave soldier marched off to a dull war. On the wagon seat she sat very straight. She had a feeling, half dread and half pride, that her life had just turned a page. Amy slept that night at Aunt March’s, in a strange, neat room. She cried a little, and then she slept like the brave.

chapters.title: Chapter 17 · Amy's Little Will
chapters.artPrompt: a young girl with golden curls writing at a small desk by candlelight in a stiff parlor with dark furniture and a parrot cage, her face thoughtful, small keepsakes laid out beside her, quiet lamplight, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Aunt March’s house was stiff, dark, and full of rules. There were French lessons, backboard exercises, and long silks to sew. Amy was homesick for the noise and love of home. Only Estelle, the French maid, was kind to her. There was a parrot too, who said rude things in French, and Amy was told not to laugh. Aunt March talked a great deal about her own will and her fine jewels. Amy listened with wide eyes, and learned more than she knew.
Amy divides her small treasures by candlelight and writes each name with care.

One quiet night Amy took out her treasures: her little books, her drawings, her best ribbons, her small keepsakes. Then she wrote her own little will, in her best hand. This to Meg, this to Jo, this to Beth. And her dearest keepsake to Laurie, with a loving word for each. She read it over twice. It made her cry a little and feel warm at the same time. That is a very odd feeling, but a true one.
Question for you: Amy gave her best things away on paper, to people she loved. What would you leave, and to whom?

When Aunt March found the paper, she read it twice and looked strangely pleased. “The child has sense,” she said, which was high praise indeed. Amy learned something the will could not say. Her treasures were never so precious as when they were promised away to the people she loved. After some weeks she went home, taller, braver, and twice as fond of the noisy little house. She kept the little will in her workbox for years, and smiled whenever she found it. And Jo, who had missed her more than she confessed, teased her and hugged her in the same minute. It was the first time Amy had ever been homesick so far from home. She learned that loving people and having them near are two different things, and the second is the dearer.

chapters.title: Chapter 18 · A Mother's Secret
chapters.artPrompt: a mother in a gray dress and cap talking earnestly by the fireside with a tall girl in a plain dress whose face is stormy with feeling, sewing basket between them, a quiet parlor with a small fire, warm evening light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: One soft evening Mother called Jo to the fireside for what she called a confidential talk. Jo came with her heart thumping, for she had her own secret and feared Mother had heard of it. The fire crackled. Mother took both her daughter’s hands. Jo braced herself like a small ship before a wave. Then Mother spoke quietly, and it was worse and better than Jo had guessed. The evening was very still, and the fire made small shadows on the wall.
Mother tells her secret, and Jo’s fierce heart stands guard over her sister.

Mr. Brooke had spoken to her of Meg, tenderly and honorably, and asked leave to hope. Mother asked Jo to help Meg choose freely. She was not to push her toward the young man, nor to pull her away. “I want Meg at home forever!” cried Jo. “She is too young to be anybody’s wife!” Mother only smiled. She reminded Jo that Meg’s life was her own, and that love given freely outlasts love commanded. Jo groaned like a ship in ballast.
Talk together: Jo wants to guard her sister, and Mother wants to free her. Who is right, or are both right together?

Still, she promised to be fair. She declared she would earn and save until Meg need not marry anybody in a hurry. Mother let her keep that comfortable plan, and hid a smile in her sewing. Upstairs Meg sang at her work, innocent as a bird. Downstairs two quiet plotters kept her secret safe. Jo began that very week to save her story money in a little tin box. The box was for Meg, though Meg never knew it. And the little house held its breath for what the spring would bring. When the talk was done, Jo went out into the dark garden and looked at Meg’s window. The light was still on, and Meg was still singing. Jo made a solemn promise to the window, and kept it all her days.

chapters.title: Chapter 19 · Laurie Makes Mischief
chapters.artPrompt: a boy in a smart suit writing a letter with a mischievous grin in a panelled study, quill in hand and an ink pot beside him, a wicked little smile curling his mouth, firelight on bookshelves, warm evening light with a hint of trouble, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Now Laurie had a fault the whole town knew: when he was bored, he was dangerous. Left alone one rainy week with nothing but his lessons, he grew restless as a cat in a barrel. A wicked idea popped into his head. He took up his quill and wrote a little love letter, mocking sweet. Then he sent it to Mr. Brooke as if it had come from Meg. The letter was so silly that only a bored boy could have written it. He stamped it, dropped it in the box, and whistled away, well pleased with himself.
The quill flies, and a joke sets out on the wet street to make trouble.

Mr. Brooke, stirred by the letter, came straight to Aunt March’s house, where Meg was visiting, to set the matter right. Their talk left Meg red, confused, and secretly glad at heart. Aunt March sniffed trouble like a weasel, and asked sharp questions that got no answers she liked. And in the middle of it all Mrs. March arrived at the door. Meg fled upstairs with her face burning like a small fire. The rain kept falling on the two gardens, on the mansion, and on one boy’s fast-cooling fun.
New word: mischief — play that goes too far and hurts someone. It always looks funny first and shameful after.

Laurie soon heard what his joke had done. He went white, then very red. Then he did the bravest thing he knew. He ran straight to Jo and confessed everything, before anyone else could tell her. He stood before his best friend, twisting his hat, ready for the storm. Jo’s temper, as we know, was a fire that leaped before it thought. And the storm, when it came, was worth every thunderclap. For once in his easy life, Laurie was afraid of a girl. The letter crossed the town through the rain, and the rain, which is honest, told nobody.

chapters.title: Chapter 20 · Jo Makes Peace
chapters.artPrompt: a girl with wavy hair scolding a tall boy under a bare tree in a snowy garden, the boy standing humbly with his cap in his hands, their breath showing in the cold air, a gray mansion beyond, soft winter light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Jo scolded Laurie as he had never been scolded in his life. “You had no right!” she cried, marching up and down the frosty garden. “Love is not a toy for bored boys! Meg’s heart is not your game!” Laurie stood and took it all, which was more than most boys could have done. Every word sank into him like rain into dry ground. The cold air stung, but the words stung more. Twice Laurie tried to speak, and twice Jo waved him down.
A hard scolding in the cold, and not one step backward from the truth.

Then Laurie went and did his best to mend it. He went to Mr. Brooke and confessed that the letter was his own foolish trick, and asked pardon like a man. Afterward he came back and stood before Jo again, humbled but steady. “I have told the truth,” he said. “It made a muddle, and I am sorry. And I will never tease about love again as long as I live.” Jo believed him, for she knew his face now as well as her own.
Talk together: Laurie made a joke that hurt three people. What is the difference between being punished and making a thing right?

Jo looked at him a long moment. Her anger was like a fire in the wind, hot one minute and gone the next. “Shake,” she said at last. And they shook on a new law between them: never touch love with a joke. Then they walked home in the dusk, best friends again, each one a little wiser than at breakfast. Jo had meant to stay angry for a week. She managed about ten minutes, and was cross with herself for it. And the frosty garden kept their secret, as gardens do. That evening Laurie sent over a hamper of chestnuts for the whole family, with no card at all. Mother knew what the chestnuts meant, and laughed till she cried.

chapters.title: Chapter 21 · Meg's Answer
chapters.artPrompt: an elegant old lady in rich velvet and a lace cap questioning a young woman in a simple dress who stands very straight before her, a grand parlor with heavy curtains and portraits, the girl's chin lifted with quiet courage, strong window light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Aunt March came swooping down on Meg like a fine old hawk. She had heard everything, and she put her questions like pins. Would Meg throw herself away on a poor tutor? Did she know that Mr. Brooke had nothing but his salary and his books? Meg sat with her hands folded and her heart beating hard. She said little, which Aunt March took for doubt. The old lady had a way of looking at people that made them feel like furniture she was pricing.
Aunt March offers Europe and fine gowns, and watches for a weakness.

Then Aunt March played her best card. She offered to take Meg to Europe. She would dress her like a lady and make her fortune. There was one condition: Meg must give up the poor young man. Something hot woke in Meg then, hotter than pride. Nobody might sneer at her honest, poor, loving friend and go unpunished. She stood up straight as a young pine. She said no, quietly, so that it sounded like thunder. And Aunt March, for once, had no answer ready.
Question for you: Aunt March offered the world, and Meg chose a plain room with love in it. Which would be harder to refuse, and why?

The old lady marched off in a huff to sulk. In her secret heart, though, she liked Meg the better for it. Meg promised herself to Mr. Brooke, and the family’s joy poured out like sunshine. The young tutor worked double hours on a small cottage. Jo was not sure whether to scold Meg for marrying or hug her for being brave. So she did both. And she found that her storm had blown over into a kind of spring. But the year’s best surprise was still waiting, folded in a letter with a war-stamp on it. Brooke came that evening to thank her, and could not speak at all, which was answer enough.

chapters.title: Chapter 22 · A Wonderful Letter
chapters.artPrompt: a family group in a small parlor around a father's letter held high by a girl in a green dress, faces shining with joy, a mother in a gray dress covering her mouth with her hands, sewing and sheet music swept aside on the table, bright morning light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Early in December a letter came with a strange, wonderful weight. Father was well. Father was coming home — for Christmas. The letter went round the table three times. The third time nobody read it, because they were all hugging too hard. Mother laughed and cried together. Beth quietly kissed the little worn paper, as if it were a bit of Father himself. Father’s handwriting shook a little at the end, and Mother said that was joy. And for once nobody told anyone not to be silly.
One letter, passed from hand to hand, turns the house upside down with joy.

After that the house burst into motion like a beehive stirred. Jo scrubbed floors till they shone and wrote a welcome speech she dared not read aloud. Meg baked until the kitchen smelled like a bakery. Amy practiced a graceful welcome in front of the glass. Beth, still thin from the fever, sewed little gifts in secret and hummed at the piano all day long. Twice the pie burned because nobody remembered it. Nobody cared. Even the cat seemed to know that something great was coming up the road.
Talk together: one year of work and worry is about to be paid for with one happy homecoming. What would you put on the table for such a homecoming?

Laurie was told, and old Mr. Laurence sent over good things for the feast. Next door and next door’s mansion were busy as one. The night before the great day, the house stood shining from cellar to garret. The table was laid, the tree was hidden, and four sisters lay awake in the dark, listening for the morning. The sisters compared speeches in whispers. They fell asleep laughing without meaning to. The morning came, as mornings do — but this one brought more than daylight. The letter went up to Mother’s room, and came down smelling of lavender. Beth slept with it under her pillow, and nobody said anything about that either.

chapters.title: Chapter 23 · Father Comes Home
chapters.artPrompt: a thin father in a worn soldier coat standing in a small parlor doorway with his travel bag set down, four daughters rushing toward him with open arms, the youngest pale girl holding his hand, the mother laughing with tears, a small Christmas tree glowing, warm evening light, joyful storybook illustration

blocks.text: At dusk on Christmas eve, slow steps came up the walk. A tall, thin man in a worn soldier coat stood in the doorway with his travel bag at his feet. For one whole moment nobody could speak or breathe. Then all five of them reached him at once, arms and laughter and tears together. The little hall was so full of love it could hardly hold it all. And the travel bag fell in the snow and stayed there, forgotten.
Beth slips her hand into Father’s and does not let go all evening.

Father was thin and brown from the war. His voice was a little rusty from so little use, but it was Father’s own voice. Beth slipped her hand into his and did not let go once all the evening. Mother held his arm as if he might step away into a dream. And Laurie came running over from the mansion to shake his hand like a man. Old Mr. Laurence sent over his very best wine and his very best wishes.
Talk together: a whole year has changed each sister. How is Jo different now from the girl who lost her temper on the frozen pond?

They kept Christmas all over again, with a small tree and Father’s stories. Nobody was tired until far into the night. Jo looked round the fire at her family and understood at last what she was worth. “It is not a splendid house,” she said to Laurie. “But it is the happiest one in town.” And everyone who heard her agreed, and said so, and meant it. Outside, the snow went on falling gently. It fell on both gardens, on the mansion, and on the little gray house that was richest of all. Father looked round the little parlor at his four daughters. His eyes went from one to another as if he were counting treasure. Then he sat down in his own chair, and the chair knew him at once.
